title: API 580 Training in Los Angeles: RBI Exam Prep Online
description: Self-paced API 580 exam prep for Los Angeles RBI teams: Cal/OSHA damage mechanism reviews, CalARP Program 4 and terminal tank rules. Instructor Q&A.
h1: API 580 Training in Los Angeles: Risk Based Inspection Exam Prep for South Bay Refinery and Terminal Teams
html:
API 580 exam prep for RBI teams in the Los Angeles basin

Risk-based inspection in Los Angeles is shaped by California law as much as by API Recommended Practice 580. The South Bay refineries work under a state process safety standard that requires formal damage mechanism reviews, the harbour terminals answer to air district tank rules with fixed inspection frequencies, and the region's refining footprint is changing. API 580 candidates here are usually inspection planners, corrosion and materials engineers, mechanical integrity engineers and senior inspectors who maintain or approve RBI plans at refineries, terminals and the contractors that serve them.

There is no Atlantis classroom in Los Angeles. The Atlantis API 580 course is a self-paced online course with instructor Q&A, built on the API 580 Body of Knowledge and RP 580 itself. API administers the examination and issues the API 580 certification, and each candidate applies to API directly. Atlantis is not an API-approved training provider, and passing the exam is a matter between you and API.

Damage mechanism reviews under section 5189.1

Title 8, section 5189.1, Cal/OSHA's process safety management standard for petroleum refineries, became operative in October 2017. Its subsection (k) requires a damage mechanism review, or DMR, for each existing and new process in which a damage mechanism exists. The rule required at least half of the initial reviews within three years of its effective date and the rest within five, and each DMR must now be revalidated at least once every five years. A DMR is also reviewed as part of a major change, and carried out before approval if the change may introduce a new mechanism.

The content requirements read like the front end of an RBI assessment. A DMR has to assess process flow diagrams, identify the potential damage mechanisms, confirm that materials of construction suit the application, specify methods to prevent or mitigate damage and review the operating parameters that could speed it up or slow it down. It must also take in inspection history, damage data, industry experience and applicable standards. The team needs expertise in engineering, equipment and pipe inspection, damage mechanisms and process operation, plus one member who knows the DMR methodology being used, and employees take part.

That is close to what RP 580 calls damage mechanism screening and the data-gathering steps behind probability of failure. The two are still different things. The DMR is a legal requirement with its own report, recommendations that must be implemented and records kept for the life of the process unit; RBI is a methodology an owner chooses, which can use the DMR as its starting point. The API 580 exam tests RP 580, not section 5189.1, so learn RP 580's vocabulary for the ideas you already use. The damage mechanism review explainer compares the two approaches in more depth.

CalARP Program 4 and the wider rulebook

The same refineries also sit under CalARP Program 4, the California Accidental Release Prevention programme level written for petroleum refineries, found in Title 19 of the California Code of Regulations, Article 7. CalEPA oversees the programme statewide, and refinery operators submit annual process safety performance indicator reports to CalEPA and to their local Unified Program Agency. For an RBI engineer, the practical result is that a refinery's process safety records can face review by more than one agency, so the documentation has to stand up on its own.

RP 580 makes the same demand for its own reasons: an assessment should be documented well enough to be audited, repeated and updated. Exam questions on documentation, the RBI team and management of change are easier for anyone who has prepared a California refinery for an audit.

What an RBI model looks like at a South Bay refinery

EIA's January 2026 refinery survey lists four large refineries in the Los Angeles area: Marathon's Los Angeles refinery at Carson and Wilmington, Chevron El Segundo, PBF Energy's Torrance refinery and Valero's Wilmington refinery. Each runs a delayed coker, a fluid catalytic cracker, alkylation and sulfur recovery, and three of them run catalytic hydrocrackers. An RBI model for a plant like that carries thousands of items, and the damage side is dominated by familiar refinery mechanisms:

  • sulfidation in hot crude, vacuum and coker sections, and naphthenic acid corrosion where crude properties support it;
  • ammonium bisulfide and chloride corrosion in hydroprocessing reactor effluent systems, and corrosion in crude unit overheads;
  • wet H2S damage, amine cracking and sour water corrosion in gas plants and treating units;
  • alkylation acid service, and high temperature hydrogen attack screened against API RP 941;
  • corrosion under insulation and external chloride cracking at units close to the coast.

The consequence side is shaped by geography. These refineries sit inside a dense urban area, with homes, schools, freeways and the port close to the fence, so the people, environmental and business consequences of a release weigh heavily. RP 580 expects the team to decide how consequence will be measured before it ranks anything, and a Los Angeles candidate should be ready to explain how the choice of consequence measures changes which items rise to the top of the matrix.

Closures, conversions and reassessment triggers

EIA reports that Phillips 66 stopped refining at its Los Angeles refinery in October 2025; the company has hired developers to study future uses of the Carson and Wilmington land. EIA also reports that Valero's Benicia refinery in Northern California has stopped refining, and plants that stay open may change crude supply or product slates as the market shifts. Each of these events touches an RBI programme:

  • A feed or crude change can introduce or accelerate damage mechanisms, which RP 580 treats as a reason to reassess and which section 5189.1 treats as a reason to review the DMR.
  • Equipment that is idled or mothballed still deteriorates, often by different mechanisms than in service, and its plan cannot simply be paused.
  • Units brought back into service, or converted, need their assumptions rechecked against the new operating window before the old risk ranking is trusted.

The examination asks what should trigger reassessment and why an RBI plan is a living document. Candidates who have watched a Los Angeles unit change service have a ready example for every one of those questions.

Tanks and terminals: where RBI meets fixed frequencies

RBI is not free to set every interval. API 653 lets an owner set internal inspection intervals for aboveground storage tanks by risk-based methods, but 49 CFR 195.432 requires pipeline operators to inspect their steel breakout tanks to API 653 while barring that risk-based alternative interval. PHMSA proposed in June 2026 to allow risk-based internal intervals for breakout tanks, with maximum limits, so check whether a final rule has changed this before relying on it. Air quality rules add their own calendar. Rule 1178 of the South Coast Air Quality Management District, which covers storage tanks at the larger petroleum facilities in the basin, requires semiannual rim seal gap measurements on external floating roof tanks, and on domed and internal floating roof tanks a complete gap measurement each time the tank is emptied and degassed and at least once every ten years. Rule 463 is the district's general rule for organic liquid storage tanks.

An RBI plan at a harbour terminal or refinery tank farm therefore has to sit inside these fixed obligations and can only optimise what is left. RP 580 expects exactly that: regulatory requirements are an input that the RBI result does not override.

A closed-book scenario from a coastal unit

The API 580 exam has no calculation section, but it does ask you to reason about cases like this practice example, which describes no real plant. Two items sit in the same unit near the harbour:

  1. Item A is a carbon steel diesel line, insulated, cycling between ambient temperature and about 250°F, with damaged jacketing in places. Its consequence category is moderate, but its probability of failure is high because the conditions favour corrosion under insulation and nobody has looked under the insulation for years.
  2. Item B is high-pressure piping downstream of a hydrocracker reactor, in hydrogen with some H2S. It has a good inspection history and a low probability of failure, but a release would be flammable, toxic and hard to isolate, so its consequence category is the highest on the matrix.

Both can land in a high-risk cell. For Item A, inspection lowers risk directly: an effective CUI campaign, such as insulation removal at the most likely locations backed by a suitable screening method, reduces uncertainty about the damage state and moves the item down the probability axis. For Item B, more inspection changes little because the risk is consequence-driven; mitigation such as better detection, faster isolation or lower inventory is what moves it. A typical exam question gives you the two descriptions and asks which action reduces risk for which item, and the wrong answers usually treat inspection as a cure for consequence.

Who sits API 580 in Los Angeles, and how they qualify

Holders of a current API 510, API 570 or API 653 certification qualify automatically, which is the usual route for experienced inspectors. Engineers and analysts without an inspector certification qualify through education plus petrochemical industry experience within the last 10 years: one year with a bachelor's degree in engineering or technology, two with a two-year degree or certificate, three with a high school diploma and five or more with no formal education. Because the requirement is petrochemical experience rather than work for an authorized inspection agency, corrosion engineers and reliability analysts at the refineries and terminals here can sit API 580 without ever holding an inspector certificate.

Studying for a closed-book RP 580 paper from Los Angeles

API 580 is 90 multiple-choice questions, 80 scored and 10 unscored pretest items, in 3.25 hours, closed-book, against a set passing scaled score. API's programme page says the exam can be taken at a test centre or by remote proctoring; check which options apply to your window when you apply. Prometric lists test centres in and around Los Angeles for candidates who prefer a centre.

API's 2026 Body of Knowledge names a single reference, RP 580, 4th edition (2023) with Addendum 1 (2025). Because nothing goes into the room, study is about understanding and precise terms. Read RP 580 through once for structure, then work through it section by section with the course notes, writing your own definitions of probability of failure, consequence of failure, inspection effectiveness and risk management. Practise explaining each idea with an example from your own unit, then check the explanation against the text. When a definition in RP 580 differs from the way your company's RBI software or procedures use the same word, send the question to the instructor: the exam follows RP 580's wording, and the answer is easier to remember once someone has shown you where the two part ways.

Exam preparation is not an RBI study

The course prepares you to pass API 580. It does not assess any of your equipment, and an API 580 certificate on its own does not make anyone an RBI practitioner; a real assessment needs data, a qualified team and the owner's approval. If your site needs an assessment rather than a certificate, Atlantis also runs remote RBI studies, described on the RBI in Los Angeles and Long Beach page. Atlantis does not offer fitness-for-service assessment, and remaining-life decisions that require it stay with the owner's engineers.

Sponsoring API 580 candidates from a Los Angeles site

Refineries preparing staff for DMR and RBI team roles, and terminal operators building integrity teams, often enrol several API 580 candidates together, sometimes alongside API 510, 570 or 653 candidates. Each person works through the course at their own pace with the instructor, and fees are quoted on request. Each candidate still applies to API individually, with their own record of experience or a current inspector certificate.

faq.q: Does Cal/OSHA require DMR team members to hold API 580?
faq.a: No. Section 5189.1 requires the damage mechanism review team to have expertise in engineering, equipment and pipe inspection, damage mechanisms and process operation, plus a member who knows the methodology, but it names no certification. API 580 is one way an engineer or inspector can show RBI knowledge, and some owners ask for it in RBI roles, so check your own site's procedures.

faq.q: Is a damage mechanism review the same as an RBI assessment?
faq.a: No, although they overlap. A DMR under section 5189.1 identifies the damage mechanisms for a process, confirms materials, sets prevention and mitigation methods and produces a report with recommendations. An RBI assessment goes on to estimate probability and consequence of failure, rank risk and plan inspection. A good DMR is an excellent basis for the damage side of an RBI model.

faq.q: Can I take API 580 at home in Los Angeles instead of at a test centre?
faq.a: API's programme page says API 580 can be taken at a test centre or by remote proctoring. Remote proctoring has its own rules for the room, computer and identity checks, and the options can differ between windows, so confirm what API offers for yours when you apply. If you would rather sit it at a centre, Prometric lists test centres in and around Los Angeles.

faq.q: I already hold API 570. Do I need to document experience again for API 580?
faq.a: A current API 510, API 570 or API 653 certification makes you eligible for API 580 automatically, so you do not need to show the petrochemical experience a candidate without one would. You still apply to API for the API 580 exam and sit it under API's rules. Many South Bay piping inspectors add API 580 once their sites start using risk-based intervals.

faq.q: Can RBI extend inspection intervals for breakout tanks at Los Angeles terminals?
faq.a: Not for pipeline operators' breakout tanks. 49 CFR 195.432 requires steel breakout tanks to be inspected to API 653 but excludes the risk-based alternative internal inspection interval. That is the rule as it stands: a PHMSA proposal published in June 2026 would allow capped risk-based intervals, and it changes nothing until a final rule takes effect. Tanks outside pipeline jurisdiction can use API 653's risk-based provisions, but air district seal and degassing inspections under South Coast AQMD rules still run on their own schedule.

faq.q: How is API 580 different from API RP 581?
faq.a: RP 580 sets out the elements of a risk-based inspection programme and is what the API 580 exam is built on. RP 581 is API's quantitative method, with detailed calculations of probability and consequence of failure. API's Body of Knowledge lists RP 580 as the only reference publication, so the questions come from RP 580, which describes quantitative RBI as one approach; RP 581's formulas are not examined.

faq.q: Does the API 580 course cover California rules?
faq.a: The course follows the API 580 Body of Knowledge, which is built on RP 580 and does not test state law. Pages like this one explain how section 5189.1 and CalARP Program 4 relate to RP 580 so that Los Angeles candidates can connect the two, and the instructor can help you map a site procedure to RP 580's terms, but exam answers always come from RP 580.
